# CLIs and developer tools: where to start

What scripts and users can rely on (flags, output, exit codes, error messages) and how failures travel from deep code to one clear message and exit status.

Flags: **C** contested (offer it as a choice, with both sides) · **A** agents do this readily · **T** has a one-file tell · **E** has a pseudo-code example.

Axes in brackets: ⊕ the lens's primary effect, the reason to reach for it · + also helps · − costs. Laws name the axes they bear on. See [AXES.md](../AXES.md).

`{kinds}`: where it matters most. `langs:` which languages have notes. `→` related lenses.

## Probes for the interview

Find first, in the code, docs, git history, CI and config. Ask only what the repository can't tell, in the project's own terms, with the evidence and a recommendation. Skip the question when the findings settle it. Also see the general stances in [THINKING.md](../THINKING.md).

### 1. Hyrum's law, Breaking-Change Surface

**Find:** For each command: what it writes to stdout and to stderr, whether it has a machine-readable mode (--json, --porcelain, a stable format flag), and which exit codes it can return and where they are defined. Which of these the README, --help text, man page or changelog promise. Tests that pin output (golden files, snapshots, subprocess tests). Scripts, CI jobs or shell completions in the repo that parse the output. Commits or issues where an output change was reverted or called breaking.

**Ask:** "<commands> have a documented <JSON mode / exit codes> in <doc>. The plain-text output of <commands> isn't promised anywhere, but <scripts / issues / CI jobs> parse it. Should changing that text count as breaking? I'd treat <JSON output and exit codes> as the contract and say in the docs that text output may change, because <who parses what>."

**Settled when:** The docs already say which output is stable, tests pin exactly that, and nothing in the repo or its issues parses the rest. The agent states the contract it found and asks only whether it holds going forward. Whether undocumented output people already parse counts as a promise is never settled by code alone.

### 2. Principle of least astonishment, Fail fast

**Find:** Trace how an error deep inside each command reaches the user: where it is caught, how it is printed (one top-level handler, per command, a raw stack trace), and which exit code comes out. Group commands by behaviour and list the ones that differ from the majority, including any that exit 0 after a failure. Whether --help or the docs list exit codes.

**Ask:** "<N> of <M> commands send errors through <handler> and exit <code>; <commands> <print a stack trace / exit 0 on failure> (<files>). Are those deliberate? I'd make <handler> the only way out for every command, with <exit-code scheme>, because a script can then tell <usage errors> from <runtime failures>."

**Settled when:** Every command already goes through one handler with a documented exit-code scheme. The agent confirms that in one line and asks nothing unless an outlier turns up.

### 3. Not Invented Here, Chesterton's fence

**Find:** Home-grown code that overlaps the standard library or a well-known package: argument parsing, config loading, colour and TTY detection, logging, retries, path handling. For each: size, when it was added (git log), who wrote it, and any commit message, comment or doc that says why. The dependency list and its history, and any stated policy such as zero dependencies or a startup-time budget.

**Ask:** "<module> does what <stdlib / package> does (<size>, added <when>; <the commit says why / no reason recorded>). Keep it and point new code at it, or move to <package>? I'd <keep it / switch> because <dependency weight / startup time / behaviour it adds that the package lacks>."

**Settled when:** A doc, comment or commit records the reason, such as a zero-dependency rule. The agent cites it and asks only whether it still holds.

### 4. Production Bugs, Developers Not Writing Tests

**Find:** Fix commits and linked issues over the last year or so, sorted by where the fix landed: flag and input parsing, the output scripts read, or deeper logic. Which fixes came with a regression test. Whether any test runs the built binary end to end (a subprocess, golden files) rather than calling functions.

**Ask:** "Of the last <N> fixes, <k> were in <area> (<examples>), and <j> came with a test. <No test / Only <tests>> run the built binary. Did bugs reach users that don't show here? I'd add <end-to-end tests over the binary for argument parsing and output> as the rule for new commands, because that's where fixes cluster."

**Settled when:** Never fully: the history shows fixes, not which ones reached users. When issues are linked to fixes, the ask shrinks to confirming the pattern the agent found.
